title: Misplaced Modifiers
intro: Place descriptions next to the person or thing they describe.

sections.heading: The core rule: stay next to what you describe
body: Place a descriptive phrase beside the word it is meant to modify. “A steak for the customer that was cooked medium-rare” appears to describe the customer.
Move the description next to steak. Read the whole sentence and ask which word the phrase actually describes.

examples.text: She returned the sweater with a torn sleeve to the clerk.
examples.label: Modifier sits next to 'sweater'

examples.text: She returned the sweater to the clerk with a torn sleeve.
examples.label: Now the clerk has the torn sleeve

sections.tip: Name the noun the phrase describes, then make sure they touch.

sections.heading: Opening phrases with a comma
body: An opening description usually belongs to the main clause’s subject: who or what the sentence is about. Identify who performs the action or has the condition, then put that subject after the comma.
“Running to catch the bus, my backpack slipped” gives the backpack the running action. “Running to catch the bus, I felt my backpack slip” supplies the runner.

examples.text: Exhausted after the marathon, Devon took a long nap.
examples.label: Devon was the exhausted one

examples.text: Exhausted after the marathon, a long nap was taken by Devon.
examples.label: A nap cannot be exhausted

sections.tip: Read the opening phrase, then check the first noun after the comma. They must match.

sections.heading: Modifiers without commas
body: Place only, nearly, almost, or just close to what it limits. Their position can change the claim.
“I nearly watched the entire series” suggests I almost watched it. “I watched nearly the entire series” says I watched almost all of it. Match the stated intended meaning.

examples.text: I watched nearly the entire series in one weekend.
examples.label: Watched almost all of it

examples.text: I nearly watched the entire series in one weekend.
examples.label: Almost watched it, but didn't

sections.tip: Limiting words (only, nearly, almost, just) go directly before what they limit.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Choices that rearrange the noun after an opening phrase often test modifiers.

Read the phrase, identify who does the action, then check the sentence’s subject. A choice may put the real doer at the end, as in “an error was found by the accountant.” The opening description still needs to fit the subject, error.

examples.text: While reviewing the budget, the accountant found an error.
examples.label: The accountant did the reviewing

examples.text: While reviewing the budget, an error was found by the accountant.
examples.label: An error did not review the budget

sections.tip: Same words, shuffled order? It's a modifier question. Put the doer right after the comma.

check.stem: Soaring above the canyon, [[the photographer captured the eagle]].
check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
choices: the photographer's camera captured the eagle
the eagle glided into the photographer's frame
capturing the eagle was the photographer's goal
check.explanation: 'Soaring above the canyon' must describe the first noun after the comma, and only 'the eagle glided into the photographer's frame' puts a soaring creature there. 'The photographer,' 'the photographer's camera,' and 'capturing the eagle' were not soaring above the canyon.

check.stem: Frozen solid overnight, [[we could skate across the pond]].
check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
choices: the pond was safe for us to skate across
skating across the pond was finally possible
we found the pond thick enough for skating
check.explanation: 'Frozen solid overnight' describes the pond, so 'the pond was safe for us to skate across' must follow the comma. In the choices that begin 'we could skate,' 'we found the pond,' and 'skating across the pond,' people and an activity become the things frozen solid.

check.stem: She [[only needs]] two more points to win the match.
check.questionText: The writer wants to emphasize how few points remain before victory. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
check.explanation: To stress how few points remain, 'only' must sit directly before 'two more points,' so 'needs only' is correct. 'Only needs' attaches the limiter to the verb instead of the number, and 'needs, only,' and 'needs only,' insert commas that wrongly cut the limiter off from 'two more points.'
